— I — Provenance
The Gate · 1916
Built in 1916.
Named by Walter Hines Page.
The gate has been open since 1916.
Walter Hines Page · 1855–1918
He named it
Garran Hill.
In 1916, you could see the Carolina Hotel
from the front porch.
The trees hadn't grown yet.

Page bought the land in February 1913, sailed for London weeks later, and watched the house rise from three thousand miles away. President Wilson had offered him the ambassadorship to the Court of St. James's -- he accepted and left before the foundation was poured.

When he finally returned to Pinehurst in December 1918, he stayed at Currituck Cottage -- not Garran Hill -- and died there weeks later.

The house was built for a life he never had the chance to live.

"Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn't I?" — Walter Hines Page, Aberdeen station, December 11, 1918

In 1916, those were saplings.
Now they are a forest.
In 1916, those were saplings. Now they are a forest.
The Tufts craftsmen planted the pines. Betty Dumaine planted the sycamores and the magnolias, in 1959.
— V — Stewardship
The Second Steward · 1959–1980
Betty Dumaine
arrived in 1959
and never left.

A prominent Bostonian, she bought the house and the surrounding land for the horses and hounds she kept. She renamed it Hollycrest -- for the large native holly trees at the front of the home -- and made it her life.

She planted the sycamores. She planted the Grandiflora magnolias. She installed the camellia garden beside the front entry circle. The grounds you are looking at are, in large part, hers.

Betty Dumaine -- Thanpuying, decorated friend of the Princess Mother of Thailand -- held birthday parties for her horses, to which the children of Pinehurst were invited. She fought to save the trees in the median of Midland Road. When she died in 1980, she left the house to Duke University.

Garran Hill has that effect on people.

Someone still
puts flowers there.
At the back of the property, under a slate cover with a brass marker: MY IRISH HUNTER BLUE FOX 1946–1965. She buried him here. Beside the grave stood a four-foot statue of a blue fox -- lost after her death, but the flowers are not.
Hollycrest, 1959
